Angel Shaw is a Lead Writer and Critic on ScreenRant's TV team, covering new-release and classic TV shows across all major streaming platforms. She has been a writer with ScreenRant since 2022 and specializes in Harry Potter, The Lord of the Rings, and fantasy.
Angel holds a bachelor's degree in language interpreting and is passionate about all things culture and communication—especially in how it relates to popular media throughout history (from Shakespeare to Friends to Game of Thrones).

The Diplomat is one of those rare series that manages to turn up the volume with every installment, and season 4 is no exception. The Netflix political drama defined itself from day one as something special, centralizing Keri Russell's Kate Wyler as she attempts to carry out her job (and passion) as the US Ambassador to the UK, all while trying to work out her complicated marriage to Rufus Sewell's Hal Wyler.

The heart of The Diplomat is Kate's complicated passion for navigating the political world, beautifully paralleled by Hal's chaotic unpredictability. Her dynamic with one is precisely the same as her dynamic with the other, and given Hal's shared passion for heavy-hitting politics, there's essentially a complicated sort of threesome here. Layer this up with an endless supply of twists and just the right amount of sexiness, and it's no wonder The Diplomat has done so well every step of the way.

The big question was whether this series, created by Debora Cahn, could keep that high quality going into season 4, especially after its most monumental twist yet. The ending of The Diplomat season 3 saw Kate and Hal go through yet another reconciliation following their private separation. The moment is somewhat ruined, however, by Kate's discovery that her husband, the Vice President, and President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) secretly stole a Russian apocalypse weapon right under the UK's nose.

Like every previous installment, The Diplomat season 4 jumps back into this big reveal seamlessly, and the fast-talking, intense political maneuvering begins from the very first moment. It's clear from the first episode that this Netflix drama is committing itself completely to chaos, which could have just as easily become a massive problem. However, The Diplomat manages an impossible sort of balance to pull it all off.
The Diplomat Season 4 Doesn't Neglect A Single Element
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/the_diplomat_n_s4_e1_00_04_14_18r-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=1300&dpr=1
blocks.c: Kate looking concerned in The Diplomat

blocks.x: Part of what has made The Diplomat so thrilling these years is the way that the narrative feels like a precarious sort of teeter-totter. One wrong move, and it will all come tumbling down. With each season, more elements are added to this carefully balanced platform, to the point that season 4 has almost too much going on. This time around, we aren't just wrapped up in Kate and Hal's relationship, because the president and first gentleman (Bradley Whitford) are thrown in as well. It's a rotating focus on an infinite number of tense, dangerous dynamics, and it works through every single moment.

With so much going on between Kate and Hal, Kate and Grace, Grace and Hal, Grace and Todd, Todd and Hal, and so on, it would have been all too easy for The Diplomat to lose touch with the other elements that have made the series so exceptional, but this isn't the case. The political relationship between the US and UK continues to play out through the complex goings-on of these married couples, to the point that it's not just balanced but symbiotic. The Diplomat season 4 is all poetic parallels disguised as soapy politics and relationship drama, and boy is it delicious.
The Diplomat season 4 is all poetic parallels disguised as soapy politics and relationship drama, and boy is it delicious.

Of course, there's far more to The Diplomat than just that. The complex relationships between these characters and the world of politics are layered with light touches of organic comedy, perhaps even more than previous seasons. Uncomfortable silences, subtle eye contact across the room, and overt sarcasm inspire laughs through what would ordinarily be tight tension. The Diplomat further balances this with intriguing touches of surreal artfulness, which is a delightfully new addition to season 4. So much is added, yet nothing falls through the cracks.
Bradley Whitford Gives A Standout Performance In The Diplomat Season 4
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/diplo_406_unit_00756rc-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=1300&dpr=1

I was surprised that a particular standout of The Diplomat season 4 is Bradley Whitford's performance as Todd Penn. Whitford is reliably fantastic (just look at The West Wing), so my expectations were already high, but it would have been difficult to expect just how intriguing this character could become. First Gentleman Todd Penn was promoted to series regular in season 4, and while he added great comedic touches in season 3, there's a lot more emotional weight to this character as his role becomes more central, and that has everything to do with Whitford.
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F678fd3e7b5a35-Angel-Shaw-2-2025.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

Todd is still funny, charming, and likable in a self-deprecating way, but we see him transform in The Diplomat season 4 as he becomes an official part of the scheming and maneuvering. Janney's Grace Penn (another spectacular performance) goes through her own agonizing and concerning evolution, and poor Todd is dragged along with her. The pressure put on the character brings out the best in Whitford, and I found myself leaning forward in my seat more and more each time he was featured on screen.
The Diplomat's Fourth Season Is Its Most Important Yet
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/diplo_401_unit_01299r2c-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=1300&dpr=1
blocks.c: President Penn sitting at her desk in The Diplomat

blocks.x: Among the more miraculous elements The Diplomat managed to balance with all the rest is its message. Something that has always been fun about this series is just how unbelievable it is. Political dramas are meant to be over the top, and with those added relationship dynamics, The Diplomat is more than most. What's interesting is that season 4 goes out of its way on multiple occasions to point out just how outrageous some of these events are, but the characters have no choice but to carry on. It's an awfully familiar experience, given the real-world political climate.
As necessary evils transform into borderline tyranny, the question in The Diplomat becomes whether even good characters can convince themselves to go along for the ride.

Each and every time The Diplomat season 4 inspires the thought, "okay, this could never happen," it's immediately followed by the reminder that these things are happening. Modern politics is all about what people with less power are willing to tolerate from those with greater power, and as necessary evils transform into borderline tyranny, the question in The Diplomat becomes whether even good characters can convince themselves to go along for the ride.

The political thriller uses this concept as a call to action, allowing season 4's finale to deliver the show's most powerful cliffhanger twist yet. The Diplomat has managed to make itself better with every installment, and with season 4's ambitious balance and chaotically structured message, there's every reason to believe that there's still nowhere to go but up.
All eight episodes of The Diplomat season 4 will be released October 15, 2026, on Netflix.
